headline: Businesses should model three rate-rise scenarios for FY2627: best case one hike, mid case two, worst case three before June — and stress-test revenue as well as costs
reasoning: Ord recommends that businesses revisit their FY26/27 forecasts using scenario analysis, given that the earlier base case of a single rate rise now looks increasingly unlikely. He suggests a three-scenario framework: one hike (best case), two (mid), and three (worst case) before June next year. Importantly, he notes businesses should model the impact on both costs and revenue, since rate rises are designed to suppress consumer spending.
quote: So I think they'll start off by maybe a three scenario. The best case scenario is there's only one interest rate increase for this financial year, which looks increasingly unlikely. The mid range is probably another two interest rate increases before June next year and the probably the worst case scenario is 3 increases between now and and June next year. And they need to factor that into their forecasts and how those interest rate increases might impact their business so they can better respond. And I can draw on historical information that shows what interest rate increases can do not only to their costs, but also to their revenue as well.
episode_title: Why Aussie businesses need a Plan B | the advisory

headline: Australian businesses facing a very challenging environment: rising costs, weak consumer demand particularly in consumer discretionary, plus regulatory change all hitting at once
reasoning: Gavan Ord describes the current environment for Australian businesses of all sizes as 'not great', with increased costs, softening demand especially in consumer discretionary sectors, and a wave of regulatory changes (surcharges, payday super) creating compounding pressure. Business confidence is suffering as a result, with interest rates acting as a catalyst for broader concerns.
quote: What we're hearing is it's a really challenging environment for businesses. They're facing increased costs. Demand is also a little bit concerning, particularly in consumer discretionary industries. And we're also looking at this red tape, it's everything's happening all at once. It's like that Michelle Young movie, Everything Everywhere All at Once. And I think that's what a lot of business managers, business owners feel like that there's so much happening at interest rates. It's just this catalyst for a lot of that.
episode_title: Why Aussie businesses need a Plan B | the advisory

headline: Government productivity rhetoric not matched by action; capital gains tax and discretionary trust changes distracting businesses from improving operations at the worst possible time
reasoning: Ord argues that while the Australian government has talked extensively about productivity since the election, budget measures on capital gains tax and discretionary trusts are forcing businesses to focus on restructuring for tax purposes rather than improving their operations. He calls for government rhetoric and action to align, particularly at state and federal level, with a genuine focus on productivity and restraining spending to support the RBA in fighting inflation.
quote: In the budget, there was some measures around productivity to improve productivity, but then there was the capital gains tax measures and the discretionary trust measures. And I have to say that businesses of all sizes, they've looked at the budget and they're focusing more on how do I manage this, this new environment, this new tax environment. So at the time when they should be focusing in on improving their business, managing through a difficult situation, they're actually asking our members, so how do I structure my business around this new discretionary trust change?
episode_title: Why Aussie businesses need a Plan B | the advisory
